title: Seminar · Count the cost of holding back an answer
question: Could a planner infer the fraction of correct answers withheld from the error among released answers alone?
answer: The size check releases four of eight answers. Two of the four are wrong, but the withheld set contains three of the five correct candidate answers. To recover that latter count you need reference answers for withheld questions as well. Evaluating just what a planner sees hides the cost of withholding useful results.

title: Seminar · Compare policies at the same coverage
question: Why did the complete-input policy avoid D1 but still show the wrong answer to T1? What does the matched comparison actually tell you?
answer: It happened to withhold D1, whose archived settings were missing, and to show correct P1. Accuracy is 3/4 compared with 2/4 at the same coverage of 4/8. T1 had complete inputs, but the candidate minute is 11 where the independently checked answer is 12. Input completeness alone cannot establish a correct calculation.

title: Seminar · Ask what depends on one scenario family
question: Can these eight observations establish that the complete-input policy improves answers on new kinds of changed queues?
answer: The observed reduction is one wrong answer per eight offered questions. Removing D gives zero per six. Removing H, P or T gives one per six. All of the observed reduction comes from D1. These four omission results describe the sensitivity of the conclusion to the particular families in the archive.

title: Independent task
question: The archive has a work log. The size policy used one unit per question. The complete-input policy used one lookup per question plus one unit per object when the scan settings were available. Compute total work, wrong answers shown and correct answers withheld. Which existing policy would you choose if a wrong answer costs six, a correct answer withheld costs one, and a work unit costs either 0.5 or 1? Find the break-even work-unit price.
answer:
# ID, objects, hand-checked final minute, candidate final minute,
# size-policy output, complete-input-policy output (None = withheld).
rows = [
    ("H1", 1,  7,  7,  7,  7), ("H2", 2, 11, 11, 11, 11),
    ("D1", 2, 16, 14, 14, None), ("D2", 3, 22, 18, None, None),
    ("P1", 3, 15, 15, None, 15), ("P2", 3, 18, 18, None, None),
    ("T1", 2, 12, 11, 11, 11), ("T2", 3, 16, 16, None, None),
]
stats = {}
for name, column in [("size", 4), ("complete input", 5)]:
    wrong = sum(r[column] is not None and r[column] != r[2] for r in rows)
    held = sum(r[column] is None and r[3] == r[2] for r in rows)
    work = len(rows)
    if name == "complete input":
        work += sum(r[1] for r in rows if r[5] is not None)
    stats[name] = (wrong, held, work)
    for price in (0.5, 1):
        print(name, "wrong/held/work", (wrong, held, work),
              "price", price, "loss", 6 * wrong + held + price * work)
sw, sh, st = stats["size"]
cw, ch, ct = stats["complete input"]
print("break-even work price", (6 * (sw - cw) + sh - ch) / (ct - st))
size wrong/held/work (2, 3, 8) price 0.5 loss 19.0
size wrong/held/work (2, 3, 8) price 1 loss 23
complete input wrong/held/work (1, 2, 16) price 0.5 loss 16.0
complete input wrong/held/work (1, 2, 16) price 1 loss 24
break-even work price 0.875
The size policy uses eight units, shows two wrong answers and withholds three correct ones. The complete-input policy uses 16 units, shows one wrong answer and withholds two correct ones. At price 0.5 the losses are 19 and 16, favoring complete inputs. At price 1 they are 23 and 24, favoring size. They tie at 7/8 per work unit. State the choice conditionally on this archive and these assumed costs. A claim about actual staff time would require timing data.
